messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert, a 62-year-old potter living in a small New England town, had spent thirty years coaxing beauty from clay. He and his wife, Margaret, raised two children, and their son, Daniel, had grown into a quiet, gentle man who loved working alongside his father in the studio. On a clear Tuesday afternoon two years ago, Daniel died of a sudden cardiac arrest while at work. The call came to Robert at the wheel of his truck; by the time he reached the hospital, his son was gone. There was no warning, no illness to prepare for—just a gap where Daniel’s voice used to be.

In the weeks that followed, Robert found himself moving through the house as though walking through invisible walls. He stopped going into Daniel’s room, stopping even to glance at the closed door. When Margaret left a photograph of Daniel on the kitchen counter, Robert quietly slid it into a drawer without saying a word. He began to notice that any object, any sound, any scent that carried even a trace of Daniel—the smell of wood shavings from the studio, the creak of the porch swing where Daniel used to sit—sent a cold spike through his chest. So he began to eliminate them. He moved the swing to the shed. He bought new brushes for his pottery, discarding the old set Daniel had given him for his birthday. He stopped listening to the radio station they had both enjoyed. He didn't explain these choices to Margaret; he simply made them, one by one, and hoped the silence would protect him.

What startled Robert most was what happened when something good came his way. A friend stopped by with a glazed bowl he had finished, full of praise. Robert felt a warm surge in his chest—and instantly shut it down. He turned away, muttered something about needing to clean his tools, and walked out of the room. Positive emotions had become treacherous, as though feeling even a flicker of contentment meant forgetting Daniel. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel happy, he would be punished, or worse, that the happiness would somehow erase his grief. So he refused every invitation, every opportunity for joy. Margaret suggested a weekend trip to the coast; Robert said no without explanation. The thought of planning anything—a dinner date, a doctor’s appointment, a retirement party—filled him with a low, persistent dread. He stopped making any plans at all, living day to day in a gray, uncommitted present. He told himself it was simpler that way, though it was not simpler. It was just less dangerous.

The studio, once his sanctuary, became a place of avoidance. He could not touch the clay without seeing Daniel’s hands pressing into it. He could not sit at the wheel without hearing Daniel’s laugh from the stool beside him. Within months, Robert had stopped working entirely. The wheel sat still, the kiln cold. Margaret had to take on extra hours at the library to cover the lost income, a fact that Robert knew but could not bring himself to address. He spent his days in the back room of the house, reading old magazines, feeding the woodstove, waiting for the hours to pass. Conversations with Margaret grew shorter. He knew she was hurting too, but talking about Daniel felt like pulling the scab off a wound that had not yet healed. So he said nothing.

It was Margaret who finally insisted, six months ago, that he see someone. She had found him staring at a cracked mug in the kitchen—a mug Daniel had made as a teenager—and without a word, Robert had thrown it in the trash. She wept, and for the first time he could not turn away. He agreed to come to this office because he had run out of ways to keep the world at a distance, and because the emptiness he had built around himself had begun to feel more terrifying than the grief it was meant to contain. He is afraid of what will happen if he lets himself feel—afraid the grief will swallow him whole—but he is also, in a small corner of his chest that he barely acknowledges, hoping that something else might still be possible.
